messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  (none)

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  (none)

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Marisol is a 27-year-old Latina animator who came to treatment months after leaving a physically abusive relationship with a boyfriend she had once imagined building a life with. When she describes what happened, she does not linger on the chronology of each incident so much as on the moment her sense of herself seemed to split. During the worst assault, in the apartment they shared, an argument escalated and he shoved her hard enough that she hit the edge of a table and fell. She remembers the shock less as pain than as disbelief that she had stayed in the room, kept arguing, and then tried to calm him down. In the weeks after she left, what settled in most deeply was not only fear of him but a corrosive conviction about what the violence meant about her. She had come to believe that the experience had changed her permanently for the worse, that some part of her had been damaged and could not be restored.

Since then, Marisol has understood the abuse through a harshly moral lens. She is certain that the relationship turned violent because of the way she acted—because she challenged him, because she did not leave sooner, because she kept trying to explain herself when she sensed his anger building. Although she can say abstractly that no one deserves to be hit, she does not apply that logic to herself. Instead she returns to tiny moments as if they are evidence in a case against her: the tone she used, the text message she sent, the fact that she went back after earlier incidents. In session, what pains her most is not just that he hurt her, but that she believes she participated in becoming the kind of person to whom this could happen.

That belief is tied to an equally painful sense that she violated her own values during the relationship. Marisol had always thought of herself as direct, self-respecting, and protective of other people. Now she speaks with visible shame about lying to friends who asked why she had a bruise, about minimizing what was happening to her younger sister, and about monitoring his mood so carefully that she stopped noticing her own. She cannot reconcile those choices with the person she thought she was. When she talks about staying, apologizing to him, or trying to soothe him after he had already frightened her, she does not describe those moments as survival. She describes them as proof that she betrayed herself.

These appraisals have come to dominate her daily life more than any single memory of the assaults. At the animation studio where she works, she can still complete assignments and sit through long hours refining motion and expression frame by frame, but she experiences herself differently now. She notices hesitation in ordinary interactions and interprets it as evidence that she has become weak. If a supervisor gives routine feedback, she absorbs it with disproportionate force, hearing confirmation that she is diminished. Her work has become slower because she second-guesses decisions she used to make intuitively, and she feels humiliated by needing reassurance from coworkers on details she once handled independently. Being single now does not feel like freedom to her; it feels like further proof that she is marked by what happened.

Marisol’s shame has narrowed her world. Friends have tried to reconnect, but she often declines invitations because she cannot bear the thought of being seen by people who knew her before and might, she imagines, detect what she believes was ruined. She does not describe herself as angry so much as contaminated by the relationship, as though the abuse revealed something defective that had been there all along. Even moments of competence—finishing a demanding sequence at work, paying her own rent, making it through a week without contact from him—rarely soften that conclusion. They sit beside a more entrenched conviction that she is no longer the woman she was and may never be again.

By the time she sought help, Marisol was exhausted by the constant self-accusation. What finally brought her in was a late night at the studio when she caught her reflection in a dark monitor and was struck by the thought that this damaged version of her was becoming permanent. She began to cry at her desk, not only from remembering the abuse, but from the certainty that she had failed some essential test of character and could not repair it. In coming to treatment, what she hopes for is modest and urgent: not to erase what happened, but to find out whether it is possible that she is not as ruined, culpable, and morally fallen as she now believes. What frightens her most is that therapy might confirm the opposite—that the person she became in that relationship is the person she truly is now.
